name: Proverbs
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint (Old Greek) through Brenton’s public-domain English translation. The Greek Proverbs differs from the Hebrew more than most books. It contains many extra lines not found in the Hebrew (for example after 3:16, 4:27, 6:8, 9:12, and 9:18), and a few Hebrew lines are missing from it; the more significant differences are footnoted. In chapters 24–31 the Greek also arranges the material in a different order: 30:1–14 follows 24:22; 30:15–33 and 31:1–9 follow 24:34; chapters 25–29 come next; and the poem of 31:10–31 closes the book. This translation keeps the Hebrew order. In quotations from the Septuagint, “the Lord” stands for the Greek kyrios, its usual substitute for the name Yahweh. Wisdom is personified as a woman in chapters 1–9, and the feminine pronouns of the Hebrew are kept. The poem of 31:10–31 is an alphabetic acrostic; the Hebrew letter of each verse is given in the notes. Poetry is printed line by line. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible, which here matches the Hebrew.

verses.text: The proverbs{a} of Solomon{b} son of David,{c} king of Israel:{d}

for gaining wisdom and discipline,
for grasping words of insight;

for taking in the discipline of good sense,
righteousness, justice, and fairness;

for giving shrewdness to the naive,
knowledge and discretion to the young.

The wise who hear will increase in learning,
and the discerning will acquire skill in steering,

for understanding a proverb and a figure,
the words of the wise and their riddles.

The fear of Yahweh is where knowledge begins;{e}
wisdom and discipline the foolish scorn.{f}

Listen, my son, to your father’s discipline,
and do not abandon your mother’s teaching,{g}

for they will be a lovely garland on your head
and a pendant around your neck.

My son, if sinners entice you,
do not give in.

like Sheol,{h} let us gulp them down alive,
entire, like those descending to the Pit;

we will find all kinds of precious goods
and fill our houses with plunder.

Cast your lot in among us;
one money bag for us all”;

my son, do not walk on the road with them;
keep your foot from their path,

for their feet run to evil
and hurry to shed blood.

For in vain a net is spread out
while any winged creature is watching!{i}

Yet these men lie in wait for their own blood;
they ambush their own lives.

Such are the ways of everyone greedy for gain:
it takes away the life of those who possess it.

Wisdom{j} shouts in the open air;
in the public squares she lifts her voice.

At the head of the noisy streets she calls out;
at the openings of the city gates she makes her speech:

“How long, you naive ones, will you love naivety,
and mockers delight in mocking,
and fools hate knowledge?

Because I called and you refused,
I stretched out my hand and no one paid attention,

because you brushed aside all my advice
and wanted nothing of my reproof,

I in turn will laugh at your disaster;
I will mock when dread comes on you,

when dread comes on you like a storm
and your disaster sweeps in like a whirlwind,
when distress and anguish come on you.

Then they will call me, but I will not answer;
they will look hard for me but not find me.

Because they hated knowledge
and did not choose the fear of Yahweh,

would have none of my counsel,
and spurned all my rebuke,

they will eat the fruit of their own way
and be glutted with their own schemes.

For the waywardness of the naive kills them,
and the ease of fools ruins them.

But whoever listens to me will live secure,
at ease, without dread of harm.”

notes.text: Hebrew mishle, plural of mashal, a word covering proverbs, sayings, comparisons, and parables.
Solomon, Hebrew Shelomoh, related to shalom, “peace.”
David, “beloved.”
Israel, “he strives with God” (Genesis 32:28).
Or “the first and chief part.”
The Septuagint adds “and there is good understanding for all who practice it, and reverence toward God is the beginning of perception” (compare Psalm 111:10).
Hebrew torah, “teaching” or “instruction,” the word later used for the Law.
The realm of the dead; also “the Pit” in the next line.
The meaning may be that a bird is not fooled by a trap set in plain view, unlike these men; or that the bird, seeing only the bait, flies into it anyway.

Here Wisdom (Hebrew chokhmoth, a plural form) appears as a woman calling in public, a portrait developed in chapters 8–9, where she is set opposite the “foreign woman” and Folly. The figure is often called Lady Wisdom.

verses.text:
My son, if you take in my words
and store up my commands within you,

tuning your ear to wisdom,
bending your heart toward understanding;

yes, if you call out for insight
and lift up your voice for understanding,

if you seek her like silver
and hunt for her as for hidden treasure,

then you will understand the fear of Yahweh
and find the knowledge of God.

For Yahweh is the giver of wisdom;
knowledge and understanding are the words of his mouth.

He stores up sound wisdom{a} for the upright;
he is a shield to those whose walk is blameless,

keeping watch over the tracks of justice
and protecting the road of his faithful ones.{b}

Then you will understand righteousness and justice
and fairness, every good track.

When wisdom enters your heart
and knowledge becomes a delight to your soul,

Discretion will keep watch over you;
understanding will stand guard over you,

rescuing you from the way of evil,
from men who speak perversely,

who leave the straight paths
to walk in the ways of darkness,

who delight in doing wrong
and revel in the perversity of evil,

whose paths are twisted
and whose tracks are crooked;

rescuing you also from the strange woman,{c}
from the foreign woman with her smooth talk,

who has left the companion of her youth
and forgotten the covenant of her God.{d}

For her house sinks down to death,{e}
and her paths lead to the shades of the dead.{f}

All who go in to her never return;
they do not reach the paths of life again.

Therefore follow the road of the good
and stay on the tracks of the righteous.

For the upright will dwell in the land,
and the blameless will remain in it,

but the wicked will be cut off from the land,
and the treacherous will be torn out of it.

notes.text: Hebrew tushiyyah, “sound judgment” or “success.”
Hebrew chasidim, those loyal to the covenant.
Hebrew zarah, “strange” or “outsider,” and in the next line nokhriyyah, “foreign”; in Proverbs these words describe another man’s wife, an adulteress. She appears again in 5:3–20; 6:24–35; 7:5–27.
Or “the covenant made before her God,” that is, her marriage vow.
Or “For she sinks down to death; her house…”; the Hebrew is difficult.
Hebrew repha’im, the shades, the dead in Sheol.

verses.text:
My son, do not forget my teaching;
let your heart keep my commands,

for they will add to you length of days,
years of life, and well-being.

So you will find favor and good repute
in the sight of God and of people.

Trust in Yahweh with your whole heart,
and do not lean on your own understanding.

Acknowledge him in every path you take,
and he will smooth out your roads.

Do not be wise in your own sight;
fear Yahweh and turn from evil.

It will be healing for your navel{a}
and refreshment{b} for your bones.

Give honor to Yahweh out of your riches
and out of the firstfruits of all your produce;

then your barns will be filled with plenty,
and your vats will burst with new wine.

My son, do not reject Yahweh’s discipline,
and do not resent his correction,

for Yahweh corrects the one he loves,
as a father the son in whom he delights.{c}

Happy is the person who finds wisdom,
the person who gains understanding,

for her profit is better than profit from silver,
and her yield than fine gold.

She is more precious than corals;{d}
nothing you desire can compare with her.

Long life is in her right hand;
in her left hand are riches and honor.{e}

Her ways are ways of delight,
and all her paths are peace.

She is a tree of life to those who grasp her,
and those who hold her fast are called happy.

Yahweh by wisdom founded the earth;
by understanding he set the heavens in place.

By his knowledge the depths burst open,
and the clouds drip down dew.

My son, do not let them slip from your sight;
keep sound wisdom and discretion.

They will be life for your soul
and grace for your neck.

Then you will go your way safely,
and your foot will not trip.

When you lie down, you will have no fear;
you will lie down, and your sleep will be sweet.{f}

Do not fear sudden terror
or the ruin of the wicked when it comes,

for Yahweh will be your confidence
and will keep your foot from the snare.

Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due,
when it is in your power to act.

Do not tell your neighbor, “Go away, come back later,
tomorrow I will give it,” when it is right there with you.

Do not devise evil against your neighbor
when he lives in trust beside you.

Do not quarrel with anyone for no reason
when he has done you no harm.

Do not be jealous of a man of violence,
and do not choose a single one of his ways,

for the devious are detestable to Yahweh,
but the upright are in his confidence.

Yahweh’s curse is on the house of the wicked,
but he blesses the home of the righteous.

Toward mockers he is a mocker,
but to the humble he shows favor.{g}

The wise will inherit honor,
but fools carry off disgrace.{h}

notes.text: Or “your body”; the Septuagint reads “your body.”
Literally “drink” or “moistening.”
The Septuagint reads “and he scourges every son whom he receives,” the form quoted in Hebrews 12:6.
Or “rubies” or “pearls”; the exact gem is uncertain.
The Septuagint adds “Out of her mouth comes righteousness, and she carries law and mercy on her tongue.”
The Septuagint reads “If you rest, you will be unafraid; if you sleep, you will sleep sweetly.”
The Septuagint reads “The Lord opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Greek kyrios, its usual rendering of Yahweh), the form quoted in James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5.
Or “but fools exalt disgrace”; the Hebrew is uncertain.

verses.text:
Listen, children, to a father’s discipline;
pay attention so as to learn understanding.

It is sound learning I hand on to you;
do not walk away from my instruction.

I too was once a boy in my father’s house,
young and tender, my mother’s only one,

Get wisdom, get understanding;
do not forget, do not swerve from the words of my mouth.

Do not leave her, and she will guard you;
love her, and she will keep you safe.

The beginning of wisdom is: get wisdom!
With all you have gotten, get understanding.{a}

Prize her, and she will lift you high;
she will bring you honor if you embrace her.

She will set a graceful garland on your head;
a crown of splendor she will hand to you.”

Hear, my son, and accept my sayings,
and the years of your life will be many.

I have taught you the way of wisdom;
I have led you along upright tracks.

When you walk, your stride will not be hampered,
and if you run, you will not stumble.

Seize hold of discipline and never loosen your grip;
protect her, since she is your very life.

Do not set foot on the path of the wicked,
and do not stride along the way of evildoers.

Avoid it, do not cross over to it;
turn away from it and pass on.

For they cannot sleep unless they have done wrong;
their sleep is snatched away unless they have tripped someone up.

For they eat the bread of wickedness
and drink the wine of violence.

The road of the righteous is like first light at daybreak,
glowing ever stronger until the day is full.

The road of the wicked is like thick gloom;
they cannot tell what trips them up.

My son, attend to my words;
bend your ear to my sayings.

Do not let them slip from your eyes;
keep them in the center of your heart.

For they are life to those who find them
and healing to all their flesh.

More than anything you guard, guard your heart,
for from it flow the springs of life.

Put crooked speech away from you;
keep devious lips far from you.

Let your eyes look straight ahead,
your gaze be fixed directly before you.

Make a level path for your feet to travel,
and every road you take will hold firm.

Lean neither right nor left;
keep your foot back from evil.{b}

notes.text: This verse is not in the Septuagint.
The Septuagint adds “For God knows the ways on the right, but those on the left are crooked; and he will make your ways straight and guide your steps in peace.”

verses.text:
My son, attend to my wisdom;
bend your ear to my understanding,

so that discretion stays with you
and your lips preserve knowledge.

For the lips of the strange woman drip honey,
and her palate is smoother than oil,

but in the end she is bitter as wormwood,{a}
sharp as a two-edged sword.

Her feet go down to death;
her steps take hold of Sheol.

She does not keep straight on the path of life;
her tracks wander, and she does not know it.{b}

So now, children, listen to me,
and do not turn aside from the words of my mouth.

Keep your path well away from her;
stay clear of the entrance to her house,

lest you hand over your prime to other men
and your years to a merciless one;

strangers will feast on your strength,
and your labors will go to a foreigner’s house.

You will moan when your end comes,
when your flesh and your body are wasted,

and you will say, “Oh, how I loathed discipline!
How my heart despised reproof!

I would not listen to the voice of my teachers
or bend my ear to my instructors.

I came close to utter ruin
in the midst of the assembly and congregation.”

Draw your water from a cistern that is yours,
running water out of a well that is yours.{c}

Must your springs spill out into the streets,
your channels of water into the squares?

Let them be yours alone,
not shared with strangers.

May your fountain be blessed,
and rejoice in the wife of your youth,

Why should you be intoxicated, my son, with a strange woman
and embrace the bosom of a foreigner?

For a man’s ways are in full view of Yahweh,
and he weighs{d} all his paths.

The wicked man’s own iniquities will trap him;
he will be held fast in the cords of his sin.

He will die for lack of discipline,
and through the greatness of his folly he will stagger away.{e}

notes.text: Wormwood, a plant with a very bitter taste, a byword for bitterness.
Or “so that you do not walk the level path of life; her tracks wander, and you do not know it.”
In verses 15–18 water, cistern, and fountain are images of the man’s own wife.
Or “levels.”
The Hebrew word for “stagger” is the same as “be intoxicated” in verses 19–20.

verses.text:
My son, if you have stood surety for your neighbor,
have struck hands in pledge for a stranger,

if you are snared by the words of your mouth,
caught by what your own lips have said,

then do this, my son, and get yourself free,
since you have fallen into your neighbor’s hand:
go, humble yourself,{a} and pester your neighbor.

Do not let your eyes close in sleep
or your eyelids droop.

Tear yourself loose like a gazelle from the hunter’s grip,{b}
like a bird from the fowler’s hand.

Go to the ant, you lazybones;
watch her ways and grow wise.

She has no commander,
no overseer or ruler,

yet she lays in her food in summer
and gathers her provisions at harvest.{c}

How long will you lie there, lazybones?
When will you get up from your sleep?

A little sleep, a little dozing,
a little folding of the hands to rest,

and poverty will come on you like a prowler,
and want like an armed man.{d}

A good-for-nothing,{e} a man of iniquity,
walks around with crooked speech,

winking with his eyes, signaling with his feet,
pointing with his fingers.

Perversity is in his heart; he devises evil all the time;
he lets loose quarrels.

Therefore disaster will come on him suddenly;
in an instant he will be broken beyond healing.

There are six things Yahweh hates,
seven that are detestable to him:{f}

haughty eyes, a lying tongue,
hands that shed innocent blood,

a heart that devises wicked schemes,
feet quick to run to evil,

a lying witness who puffs out falsehoods,
and one who stirs up strife between brothers.

My son, keep your father’s command,
and do not abandon your mother’s teaching.

Fasten them to your heart forever;
knot them about your throat.

For the command is a lamp, the teaching is light,
and correction that disciplines is the road to life,

keeping you from the wicked woman,{g}
from the slick tongue of the outsider.

Do not let your heart crave her loveliness,
and do not be taken in by the flutter of her lashes.

For a prostitute’s price is a round of bread,
but another man’s wife stalks a man’s very life.{h}

Can a man scoop fire into his lap
and his clothes not be burned?

Or can one walk on hot coals
and his feet not be scorched?

So it is with one who goes in to his neighbor’s wife;
no one who touches her will go unpunished.

People do not despise a thief if he steals
to fill his belly when he is hungry;

yet if caught, he must repay sevenfold;
he must give up all the goods of his house.

The man who commits adultery has no sense;
he who does so brings ruin on himself.

Blows and dishonor he will get,
and his disgrace will not be wiped away.

For jealousy kindles a husband’s rage;
on the day of vengeance he will not spare.

He will accept no compensation;
he will not be appeased though you multiply gifts.

notes.text: Or “trample yourself,” that is, swallow your pride.
Literally “from the hand”; “of the hunter” is supplied from the parallel line, as in some ancient witnesses.

The Septuagint adds “Or go to the bee and learn how diligent she is and how earnest her work is; kings and commoners use her labors for health, and she is desired and honored by all; though weak in strength, she is advanced because she honors wisdom.”
The Septuagint adds “But if you are diligent, your harvest will come like a spring, and poverty will run away like a poor runner.”
Hebrew ’adam beliyya‘al, “a man of Belial,” a word for worthlessness or wickedness.
A “six… seven” saying, a numerical pattern also found in 30:15–31.
The Septuagint reads “from the married woman.”
Or “For on account of a prostitute a man is brought to a loaf of bread.” The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.

verses.text:
My son, keep my words
and treasure up my commands within you.{a}

Keep my commands and live,
my teaching like the pupil of your eye.

Tie them on your fingers;
inscribe them on the tablet of your heart.

Say to wisdom, “You are my sister,”
and call understanding your kinswoman,

to keep you from the strange woman,
from the foreign woman with her smooth words.

From the window of my house
I looked out through my lattice,

and I saw among the naive,
I noticed among the youths,
a young man lacking sense,

passing along the street near her corner,
taking the road toward her house,

in the twilight, in the evening of the day,
in the dead of night and the dark.

And there a woman comes to meet him,
dressed like a prostitute, with a guarded heart.{b}

She is loud and unruly;
her feet never stay at home;

one moment out in the road, the next in the market squares,
at every street corner she waits in ambush.

She seizes him and kisses him;
boldfaced, she tells him,

“I had to offer peace offerings;
today I have paid my vows.{c}

So I have come out on purpose to meet you,
searching for your face, and here you are!

I have spread my couch with coverings,
colored linens from Egypt.

I have sprinkled my bed
with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.

Come, let us soak ourselves in lovemaking till dawn;
let us revel in love.

For my husband is not at home;
he has gone on a long journey.

He took a bag of money with him;
he will come home at the full moon.”

With her many persuasions she bends him;
with her smooth lips she drives him on.

until an arrow pierces his liver,
like a bird rushing into a snare,
not knowing it will cost him his life.

So now, children, listen to me;
pay attention to the words of my mouth.

Let your heart not veer toward her roads;
do not stray onto her tracks,

for many are the victims she has brought down,
and countless are all those she has slain.

Her house is the way to Sheol,
going down to the chambers of death.

notes.text: The Septuagint adds “My son, honor the Lord, and you will be strong; and besides him fear no one.”
Or “with secret intent” or “with a veiled heart.”
The meat of a peace offering had to be eaten within a day or two (Leviticus 7:15–16), so she has a feast ready.
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain; the Septuagint reads “as a dog to bonds, or as a deer shot in the liver with an arrow.”

verses.text:
Listen! Is that not Wisdom calling,
Understanding lifting up her voice?{a}

On the heights beside the road,
where the paths meet, she takes her stand;

beside the gates at the entrance to the city,
at the doorways she cries aloud:

“To you, people, I am calling;
my voice goes out to all humankind.

You naive, learn shrewdness;
you fools, learn sense.{b}

Listen, for I speak of noble things;
from my lips come upright words.

My mouth utters truth;
wickedness is detestable to my lips.

All the words of my mouth are in righteousness;
nothing in them is twisted or crooked.

They are all plain to the discerning
and right to those who find knowledge.

Take my discipline instead of silver,
knowledge rather than choice gold,

for wisdom is better than corals,
and nothing desirable can equal her.

I, Wisdom, live with shrewdness;
I find out knowledge and discretion.

To fear Yahweh is to hate evil.
Pride and arrogance, the way of evil,
and a perverse mouth I hate.

Counsel and sound wisdom are mine;
I am understanding; strength is mine.

Through me kings hold their thrones
and rulers enact just laws.

By me princes govern,
and nobles, all who judge rightly.{c}

Those who love me I love,
and those who seek me early will find me.

Riches and honor are with me,
enduring wealth and righteousness.

My fruit is better than gold, than pure gold,
and my yield than choice silver.

In the road of righteousness I go,
in the middle of the tracks of justice,

to endow with wealth those who love me
and to fill their treasuries.{d}

Yahweh acquired me{e} at the beginning of his way,
before his works of long ago.

From everlasting I was set up,{f}
from the first, before the earth began.

When there were no depths I was brought forth,
when there were no springs heavy with water.

Before the mountains were sunk in place,
before the hills, I was brought forth,

while he had not yet made the earth and the open fields
or the first of the dust of the world.

When he set the heavens in place, I was there,
when he drew a circle on the face of the deep,

when he made firm the clouds above,
when the springs of the deep grew strong,

when he assigned the sea its limit
so that the waters would not pass his command,
when he marked out the foundations of the earth,

laughing over the world, his earth,
and finding my joy among humankind.

Now then, children, hear me:
blessed are those who keep to my ways.

Listen to discipline and be wise;
do not neglect it.

Blessed is the person who hears me,
keeping watch at my gates day by day,
standing guard at my doorposts.

For whoever finds me finds life
and obtains favor from Yahweh,

but whoever fails to find me wrongs his own soul;{h}
all who hate me are in love with death.”

notes.text: Wisdom speaks in her own voice through this chapter. On the figure of Lady Wisdom, see the note at 1:20.
Literally “understand heart.”
Literally “all the judges of righteousness”; the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses read “the earth.”
The Septuagint adds “If I tell you what happens daily, I will remember to recount the things of old.”

Hebrew qanani, from qanah, which usually means “acquire,” “get,” or “possess” (as in 4:5, 7), and in a few places may mean “create” or “beget” (Genesis 14:19, 22; Deuteronomy 32:6). The Septuagint has ektisen, “created” (Brenton “made”); Aquila and other later Greek versions have “acquired” or “possessed.” The verse became central in the fourth-century debates over the nature of Christ, identified with Wisdom.
Or “woven,” as in Psalm 139:13, or “installed.”
Hebrew ’amon; or “like a little child,” reading ’amun, “nursling.” The Septuagint has “suiting myself to him.”
Or “whoever sins against me.”

verses.text:
Wisdom has built her house;
she has hewn out her seven pillars.{a}

She has slaughtered her animals, mixed her wine,
and set her table.

She has sent out her young women; she calls
from the highest points of the city:

“Whoever is naive, turn in here!”
To the one lacking sense she says,

“Come, eat of my bread
and drink of the wine I have mixed.

Leave naivety behind and live;
walk straight on in the way of understanding.”

Whoever corrects a mocker earns abuse;
whoever rebukes a wicked man gets hurt.

Do not rebuke a mocker, or he will hate you;
rebuke a wise man, and he will love you.

Instruct the wise, and they grow wiser still;
teach the righteous, and they add to their learning.

The fear of Yahweh is the start of wisdom,
and knowledge of the Holy One{b} is understanding.{c}

For through me your days will multiply,
and years of life will be added to you.

If you are wise, you are wise to your own benefit;
if you mock, you alone will bear it.{d}

Lady Folly is boisterous,
naive, and knows nothing at all.{e}

She sits at the door of her house,
on a seat at the heights of the city,

hailing the passers-by
who are keeping to the straight road:

“Whoever is naive, turn in here!”
To the one lacking sense she says,

“Stolen water is sweet,
and bread eaten in secret is delicious.”

But he does not know that the shades are there,
that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.{f}

notes.text: The seven pillars may picture a grand house, the seven days of creation, or the completeness of Wisdom’s work; the meaning is debated.
Hebrew qedoshim, plural, perhaps a plural of majesty; or “of holy ones.”
The Septuagint adds “for to know the law is the mark of a sound mind.”

The Septuagint adds three verses comparing the one who leans on lies to someone who herds the winds and chases birds in flight, abandons his own vineyard, and walks through a dry desert gathering barrenness with his hands.

Literally “A woman of folly.” Folly is drawn as Wisdom’s rival, inviting the same naive guests (compare verses 4 and 16). The second line is uncertain; the Septuagint reads “and she does not know shame.”

The Septuagint adds “But hurry away; do not linger in the place or fix your eye on her, for so you will pass through strange water. Keep away from strange water, and do not drink from a strange fountain, so that you may live long and years of life may be added to you.”
